passages.happening:
The chapter gathers David's wars into one summary. He defeats and subdues the Philistines (verse 1). He defeats the Moabites. ‘He measured off with two lengths those to be put to death, and with one length those to be spared’ (verse 2), and Moab becomes subject to David and pays him tribute.

He defeats Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, who had marched out to restore his power along the Euphrates. David captures chariots, charioteers and foot soldiers, and he hamstrings all the horses except a hundred (verses 3-4). When the Arameans of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, David defeats them too and puts garrisons among them, and they pay him tribute. ‘So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went’ (verse 6). He brings the gold shields of Hadadezer's officers to Jerusalem, and a great deal of bronze from Hadadezer's towns (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 7 promised David rest from his enemies and a great name. Chapter 8 shows that promise taking shape. The small hill kingdom Saul left behind becomes, within a generation, the leading power between Egypt and the Euphrates. These wars are usually placed in the early tenth century BC, when Egypt was divided and weak and Assyria, which would dominate the region from the ninth century on, was not yet pressing west. That left room for a regional power to rise.

The Aramean kingdom of Zobah, under Hadadezer, seems to have been the strongest state in southern Syria, with ambitions reaching toward the Euphrates. Tribute was the regular payment a subject kingdom made to its overlord, a sign of submission as much as a tax, and garrisons in Damascus and Edom enforced it.

Hamstringing captured horses disabled them for war. Israel's law forbade its king to build his power on many horses, and David keeps only a hundred.

This is a royal summary, the kind of compressed record of victories that ancient kings liked to set up. What sets it apart is the refrain: the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. The victories are credited to God, not to David's genius.
passages.later:
The law had said of Israel's king, ‘But the king must not acquire many horses for himself’ (Deuteronomy 17:16).

God had promised Abraham, “To your descendants I have given this land” (Genesis 15:18), with borders reaching to the Euphrates, and those borders came closer to reality under David and Solomon than at any other time: ‘And Solomon reigned over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines’ (1 Kings 4:21). Balaam's oracle had spoken of a ruler from Israel over Moab and Edom (Numbers 24:17-18), and the first to match it was David.
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand David's killing of two thirds of the Moabite prisoners?

Verse 2 is stark, and the text gives no reason. It is all the more puzzling because David had once trusted his parents to the king of Moab (1 Samuel 22:3-4), and his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 4:17). Some interpreters think Moab had betrayed David, though nothing in the text says so. Others read the measuring line as a kind of mercy by the standards of the day, since killing every prisoner was not unusual then, and a third are spared.

The narrator neither praises nor condemns the act. The book as a whole is unsparing about David's violence, and Chronicles later says that he could not build the temple because he had shed much blood (1 Chronicles 22:8). The Bible records David's wars as part of how God kept his promise, and it refuses to make David a model in every act. Readers are not asked to approve everything the king did, and the chapter gives no model for the treatment of any prisoner.
passages.asks: The chapter twice credits God with David's victories. Ask where you are tempted to take the credit for what you have been given. And ask what you have won that you would not want to be judged by the way you won it.

passages.t: Gifts from Hamath, and Edom subdued
passages.happening:
King Toi of Hamath hears that David has defeated Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi. He sends his son Joram ‘to greet King David and bless him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer’ (verse 10), with gifts of silver, gold and bronze.

David dedicates these to the LORD, with all the silver and gold he had taken from the nations he subdued: Edom and Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines and the Amalekites, and the plunder of Hadadezer (verses 11-12).

‘And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt’ (verse 13). He puts garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites become subject to him. Again the refrain: ‘So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Hamath lay further north, on the Orontes River. Its king welcomed the defeat of his rival Hadadezer, which is why he sends his own son with gifts. The word for tribute, minchah, is the same word used for a grain offering to God. In that world submission to a king and to a god were described in similar terms.

David's dedication of the plunder set it apart for God's house rather than the king's treasury. The gold shields and the bronze were wealth and trophies at once.

The chapter is a summary, not a sequence. The Ammonite and Aramean wars are told at length in chapter 10. Some names and numbers differ between Samuel and Chronicles, and between the Hebrew and early translations. In verse 13 the standard Hebrew reads Aram where Chronicles and the Greek translation read Edom, which the BSB follows. The two words differ by one letter that looks much like another, and a copyist could easily confuse them.
passages.later:
Chronicles says that Solomon later used David's bronze ‘with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles’ (1 Chronicles 18:8).

The Edomite war is remembered elsewhere, with different numbers. Psalm 60 is headed, ‘When he fought Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, and Joab returned and struck down 12,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt’ (Psalm 60:1), and Chronicles gives the victory to Abishai: ‘Moreover, Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt’ (1 Chronicles 18:12). Readers explain this as stages of one campaign, different commanders credited for the same victory, or a copying slip, and none is certain.

Isaac had said to Esau, the father of Edom, ‘You shall live by the sword and serve your brother’ (Genesis 27:40).
passages.asks: David gave the plunder to God instead of keeping it. Ask what you have gained that you treat as yours alone. And ask what it would look like to set some of it apart for God.

passages.happening:
‘Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people’ (verse 15).

Then come the officials: Joab over the army; Jehoshaphat the recorder; Zadok and Ahimelech the priests; Seraiah the scribe; Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites; ‘and David’s sons were priestly leaders’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
After all the wars the chapter turns, in verse 15, from conquest to government, as if to say that victory exists for the sake of just rule. Justice and righteousness are a pair. Justice means right judgment and the right ordering of a community, above all the protection of the weak in the courts. Righteousness means doing what is right within relationships, including what a ruler owes his people. Together they describe the king's highest task, and they are exactly what David will fail to do in his own house.

The list shows a real state taking shape: a commander, a recorder (probably a herald or royal secretary), priests, a scribe, and a royal guard of Cherethites and Pelethites, foreign soldiers usually linked with Crete and the Philistine coast.

The note that David's sons were priestly leaders is a puzzle, since Israel's priests came from the tribe of Levi. Chronicles calls them chief officials at the king's side, and interpreters debate whether the word here means priests in a looser sense, something like royal chaplains. A similar list of officials comes again in chapter 20, and the two lists frame the long story of David's family in chapters 9 to 20.
passages.later:
The prophets took up the same pair to describe the king to come from David's line: ‘He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore’ (Isaiah 9:7).

Chronicles gives the last line of the list differently: ‘and David’s sons were chief officials at the king’s side’ (1 Chronicles 18:17).
passages.asks: The chapter says that good power exists to do justice and righteousness for all the people. Ask what that would look like in the authority you hold. And ask who among those under you has the least power to make you listen.
